titles.111: §.V: What the Confession is we settled; of what kind forces a digression on varied editions — the αὐτόγραφον
titles.112: §.V: Or ἀπόγραφον hand-copies at the Diet — or τυπόγραφον print, private at Breslau and public at Wittenberg
titles.113: §.V: Early prints differ from one another and from the autograph — Art. X German vs Latin; Bellarmine; Schmid; Baden collation
titles.114: §.VI: Melanchthon's more polished Variata while Luther lived; repeats in 1540–42 and 1551; later public approval
titles.115: §.VI: Our writers press the case; Mentzer himself owns the Variata's later public approval as same in substance
titles.116: §.VII: To brand the Variata corrupt injures the Confession and Melanchthon; variation is essential or only accidental

latin.111:
§. V.
QUID sit Augustana Confessio, indubia quâdam Descriptione elucidavimus; QUAE autem sit, ut inquiramus, variae ejus variataeque Editiones, & ingentes de his ipsis subortae altercationes ac digladiationes efflagitant. Namque VEL Αὐτόγραφον est, seu Ἀρχέτυπον, i. e. illud ipsum Exemplar, quod Caesari exhibitum fuit; idque sive Latinum tantum, eóque unicum, à Chytraeo memoratum, Hist. August. Confess. p. 81. sive Latinum potiùs & Germanicum simul, eóque binum, Caelestino descriptum utrumque Tom. II. pag. 151. & p. 169. Ambo Exemplaria, post praelectionem Exemplaris Germanici per Cancellarium Saxonicum Christianum Pontanum factam, Caesaris manu apprehensa sunt, Germanicum Secretario Imperatoris Alexandro Sveis, Electori Moguntino offerendum, à Caesare datum, Caelest. Tom. I. p. 141. & Tom. III. p. 190. & ad Moguntinum Archivum deinceps relatum; Latinum à Caesare retentum, tandemque ad Bruxellense archivum depositum est. Utrumque in dictis archivis, multis annis latuit, teste Bellarmino, Judicio de Libro Concordiae Tom. II. Controv. p. 485.; Quin paulò post alterum [Germanicum auguror] è Tomo Actorum publicorum, in Comitiis Augustanis tum collectorum, excisum esse adserit Dorscherius, Dissert. de Providentia Divina circa August. Confess. Ao. 1555. Rostochii habitâ; ut adeò Genuinum non-variatae augustanae Confessionis Exemplum hodie, non ampliùs exstet, rectè sic inferente Baclero, Memoriali sup. cit. p. m. 406. in fine. [Nota: Justus Jonas Luthero scribit, apud Chytraeum pag. 74. in med. Caesarem sibi fecisse Confessionem Augustanam Italicâ & Gallicâ linguâ reddi, hoc verò in linguas has transferri interpretor.]
latin.112: VEL Ἀπόγραφον seu ἔκτυπον, i. e. justum, de verbo ad verbum juxta Originale, calamo intellige conceptum Exemplar, quale tempore comitiorum Augustanorum non facilè negaverim exstitisse, cùm probabile haut fiat, nec Theologos, inter hos Concinnatorem augustanae Confessionis praecipuum, Melanchthonem, nec Status Imperii, quorum nomine Confessio adornata fuit, Exemplaris, Caesari exhibendi exhibitique, exactam omnino Copiam, imò plures à singulis Statibus procuratas, habuisse, sibiique in varios perquam casus retinuisse servasseque, alioquin, & si secus fecissent, ad unum omnes, si minus supinae negligentiae, certè stupidae cujusdam improvisionis, coarguendi; VEL denique, τυπόγραφον seu Ἔκτυπον, praelô, i. e. juxta Exemplar apographum, calamo factum, typis exscripta, idque vel privato ausu, qualis eodem anno Vratislaviae, vernacula lingva in 4to, typis Adami Dyonis, prodiit, de qua Chytraeus Hist. August. pag. 47. pronunciat, ad Originalem Confessionem in Moguntino servatam Archivo, fuisse formatam, quamque idem Chytraeus ipsemet haud rarò sequitur, vid. auctor. der ausführlichen Behauptung pag. 6. in fine; Vel publica auctoritate, quales anno sequenti Wittenbergae plures, tam Germanicae, quàm Latinae, & in 4to, & in 8vo excusae sunt, primas tamen inter omnes obtinente Latinâ in quarto, etiam Vratislaviensem in praefatione sua, ceu spuriam arguente, uti observat Calovii Critic. Sacr. pag. m. 82.
latin.113: De his omnibus, praelô scil. annis duobus primis, commissis, certum est, tùm inter se, tùm ab Autographo haud rarò verbis differre: Probant enim discrimen verborum prius, non Exemplaria tantùm Wittenbergensia cum Vratislaviensi, sed & Wittenbergensia inter se, Latinum scil. in 4to, cum Germanico ejusdem formae, collata, potissimum quod ad Articulum X. attinet, etiamsi utrumque Exemplar Wittenbergense eundem Typographum Georgium Rhauium expertum sit, vid. Calovii Critic. p. à 86. ad 98. Idem probant Exemplaria Augustanae Confessionis, tam Latina, quàm Germanica, à Chytraeo & Coelestino Historiis suis illata; etiam utriusvis Auctoris Latina cum Germanicis comparata. E.g. tàm Caelestini, quàm Chytraei Germanica, Articulum X. his verbis efferunt: Vom Abendmahl wird also gelehret, daß wahrer Leib und Blut Christi wahrhaftiglich unter der Gestalt des Brods und Weins im Abendmahl gegenwärtig sey, und da ausgetheilet und genommen wird, derhalben auch die Gegenlehre verworffen wird. Tom. II. p. 53. b.; At Latina eorundem Autorum, articulum X. sic formatum habent, ut Speciei Panis & Vini nulla prorsus mentio injiciatur: De Coena Domini docent, quòd Corpus & Sanguis Domini verè adsint, & distribuantur vescentibus in Coena Domini, & improbant secus docentes. Tom. eod. pag. 172. b. Similes Discrepantias reperias circa Articulum XIII. & XVIII. in Exemplaribus Latinis Chytraei & Coelestini, se inter comparatis, utpote quorum prius, Chytraeanum scil. multa adjecta habet, quae in Coelestiniano haud inveniuntur. Ut proinde mirùm non sit, cùm Pontificios, tùm Protestantium nonnullos, de discrepantia Exemplarium conquestos subinde fuisse, nec à vero abludat Bellarminus, quando loco retrò citatô scribit, singulis propè annis, alia atque alia Exemplaria prodiisse, quae licèt omnia Confessionis augustanae titulum prae se ferrent, tamen & verbis & sententiis, tum inter se, tùm ab illa prima Confessione, Caesari exhibita, plurimum dissenserint; Quin potiùs quali quali verborum Bellarmini veritate convictus Joh. Schmidius, solius hyperboles dictionem Bellarmini infimulet, ita respondens: Quod de mutatione, singulis prope annis factâ, scribit Bellarminus, est hyperbolicon; mutatam fuisse Augustanam Confessionem non negamus, sed quoad verba tantùm, non quoad res ipsas & Sententias; Initio mutationem esse factam concedimus, quô pactô ipsi Confessionis essentiae nihil accessit vel decessit: Certum enim est, August. Confess. Anno 31. Wittenbergae editam, ratione Substantialium & Doctrinalium, ab Exemplari Augustae exhibito, nequaquam dissensisse, licèt quoad Phraseon & Dictionum additiones cum prototypo non planè congrueret. Causas mutationum variarum require apud Calovium in Crit. & pag. 85. Posterius verborum Discrimen multiplex, scil. typis expressorum exemplarium Imprimis ejus, quod Formulae Concordiae insertum ab Autographo, accurata collatione delineavit Illustriss. Princeps Ernestus Fridericus Marchio Badenensis, im Christl. Bedenck. und Motiven, die Sr. Fürstl. Gnaden von der Subscription der F. C. abgehalten. à pag. 1. ad 98. gedruckt auf dem Schloß Staffort anno 1599.
latin.114:
§. VI.
Typis exscripta Augustanae Confessionis Exemplaria succedentibus annis plura alia insecuta sunt, donec Melanchthon Anno 37. & 38. vivo adhuc Luthero aliisque Augustanae Confessionis exhibitoribus, cum varietatem exemplorum plurium observasset, de edenda expolitiori & correctiori consilium & cepit, & nemine contradicente executus est, quod e pluribus Theologi in colloquio Altenburgico pag. 404, probaturi hoc pacto istud, quod Calovius nullo documento constare scribit, Critic. pag. 202. Videatur etiam Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung. pag. 27. in fine & pag. 28. Idem Anno 1540. & 1542. repetere instituit Melanchthon; quin Anno 1551. repetitionem tertia vice, sed prolixiorem paulò, idque jussu multorum Statuum Protestantiorum confecit, in Corpore Doctrinae Melanchthonis legendam, Scriptum utile & lectu dignum, a Joh. Museo appellatum, in quô Doctrina Augustanae Confessionis perspicue & eleganter declarata sit. Praelect. in Epitom. Formul. Concord. pag. 35. Et quamvis priores duae Editiones Melanchthonianae, Approbationem publicam Antecedentem haud habuerint, habuerunt tamen Consequentem, tàm aliorum Theologorum, Chytraei, Selnecceri, Brentii, Theologorum Altenburgicorum, hosque inter Pauli Eberi, Misnicorum, Grypswaldensium, ipsius quoque Lutheri, Tomo Germanico Jenensi 7. fol. 447. collat. cum fol. 448. b. quam Statuum Imperii in Conventibus, Wormatiensi, Ratisbonensi, Francofurtensi & Nauenburgico, approbationem suam sequentibus verbis declarantium: Neque verò animus nobis est, quòd per hanc repetitionem & renovatam Subscriptionem primum excusae Confessionis, discedere ab ea quae Anno 40. exhibita, vel in minimo velimus. Cum enim illa aliquot Colloquiis, & Disputationibus cum Adversariis institutis, in aliquibus Articulis ideo copiosius explicata sit, ut Caelestis Veritas eò magis illucesceret, & fiducia in meritum Redemtoris nostri J. C. absque humanis traditionibus pura & incorrupta conservaretur & ad posteritatem transmitteretur, perinde illam sicut & aliam, deserere non possumus, praesertim cum locupletata ista, Anno 40. & 42. typis evulgata Confessio multorum nunc in manibus & magna ex parte Ecclesiis & Scholis nostris in usu sit.
latin.115: Omnia haec prolixius prosecuti sunt nostates, Hospinianus, Georgius Pauli, Sohnius, Ursinus aliique, etiam hôc locô praecipuè commemorandi tum Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 27. & 57; etiam in appendice, oder dem Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 25. ad 36. tùm Venerandus Becmannus noster, sub nomine Orthuini Gratii contra Liebhardum Cap. III. §. 2. integrô à pag. 73. ad 74. qui etiam variandae Confessionis Augustanae causas haud negligendas in medium adducit, à pag. 69. & exceptiones, Approbationi subsequenti variatae Confess. intentari solitas, nervose retundit l. cit. à pag. 73. ad 81. Crocium secutus, Comment. de Aug. Conf. Societate Cap. 54. 55. 56. cum quo etiam Cavillationes, tàm Vetustiores seu Hutterianas, in Concordia Concordi, p. m. 344. & 418. ac seqq., nec non in Anti-Peucero à pag. 7., quàm recentiores & Calovianas Crit. Sacr. à pag. 203. ad 228. enervat eluditque. Nobis hic suffecerit annotasse, etiam Balth. Mentzerum, Variatae Confessionis Oppugnatorem satis strenuum, approbationem hujus subsequentem publicam, pro qua nunc disputamus, ingenuè agnovisse, quando in Prolegom. ad August. Confess. p. m. 21. ita scribit: Qui mutatam Confessionem admiserunt, publicè testati sunt, hactenus & non aliter à se recipi, quatenus in ipsis rebus planè conveniat cum Prototypo, sicuti patet ex Hist. Conventus Navenburgici pag. 61. Hactenus Mentzerus; quod ipsum quomodo intellexerint Status Imperii, vidimus paulò ante ex Epistola eorum ad Ferdinandum primum scripta. Praeterquam quòd, vel ex adductis è Mentzero verbis, apparet, Variatam Confessionem Augustanam in ipsis rebus planè cum Prototypo convenientem habitam fuisse.
latin.116:
§. VII.
Ut proinde tam in Augustanam Confessionem ipsam, quàm in ejus praecipuum propemodum ex Theologis Auctorem, Theologorum pariter atque omnium Eruditorum Germanorum suô tempore Phoenicem faciléque Principem, optimum Melanchthonem, injurii sint qui Variatam Editionem, ceu corruptam & depravatam, cum August. Confess. primigenia haudquaquam eandem, sed ab hac prorsus aliam, clamitant. Nam Variatio isthaec vel Essentialis est, & in Fidei Fundamentum impingere dicitur, & tùm Philippus, unà cum Confessione mutata, Haereseos infimulatur; vel Accidentalis, & tùm cum primigenia in ipsis rebus planè congruit, ut loquitur Mentzerus, eóque cum ista eadem. Quâ ratione huc quadrat responsio Joh. Schmidii, Bellarmino regesta, & §. V. à nobis allata, cui adjicimus, quae idem Auctor subnectit: Quodsi, inquit, Verborum, Dictionum & Phrasium Mutatio & Variatio ipsam Confessionem tolleret, jam dudum de Symbolo Apostolico actum fuisset, quòd aliâ atque aliâ verborum serie ab aliis Ecclesiae Doctoribus propositum fuisse, monumenta testantur pag. 77. in fine & pag. 88. Praesertim, quandô ipsi Status Imperii inter duas dictas Confessiones neutiquam discriminarunt, sed utramque unam eandemque reputarunt, vid. Der Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung à p. 43. ad 52. Inepti verò habendi, qui Variatam, proptereà Augustanam esse negant, quod Augustae exhibita non fuit, porismatizante sic Mentzero: Quae Confessio Augusta exhibita non fuit, Augustanam eam dici non deberi. Proleg. n. 9. p. m. 8. etiam asseclas híc nactô, quàm plurimos, Schmidium, locô citatô pag. 12. Calovium, l. c. p. 8. aliosque. Quasi verò, nihil, quòd Augustae exhibitum non est, Augustanum dici non possit; Vel Augustana Confessio, locum Civitatemque magis, in qua facta est, quam res & Articulos, ex quibus constat, denotet respiciatve; (Dico, Confessionem August. non MAGIS Civitatem in qua facta est, quàm Articulos, ex quibus constat, denotare atque respicere, ut non negem, à Civitate ista denominari potuisse, etiam denominandam in posterum fore, licèt forte contingat, ut [quod fieri coepisse gravissimè dolemus] civitas haec Imperialis ad pagi cujusdam formam redigatur.); Vel Wittenbergae Anno 1531. in lucem edita Confessio aliaeque haud paucae mutatae, mutationemque variam, omnium Confessione, passae, non iis ipsis ampliùs Augustanae sint, qui à Philippo variatam aspernantur ac aversantur, eò, quòd Augustae non exhibitae sunt.
latin.117: Denique sibi ipsis adversi & tantum non αὐτοκατάκριτοι deprehenduntur, qui vel (1.) Confessionem Augustanam invariatam hujusque Sensum adeò ampliatum eunt, ut etiam soli Formulae Concordiae domesticas Doctrinas, e.g. de Orali Corporis Christi Manducatione, de Ubiquitate seu Omnipraesentia Corporis Christi, similesque, (de quibus ne somniavit quidem Augustana Confessio) quin totam Concordiae Formulam illacomprehenfam ajunt, expunctâ tamen variante in nonnullis, Philippicâ Confessione, Brentianis sic interpretationibus & Consequentibus locum facturi, prohibitis exclusisque Melanchthonianis. Quorsum digitum intendit doctissimus alioquin Lutheranorum Theologorum & non nisi cum veneratione mihi nominandus, Joh. Georg. Dorscheus, Disp. Seculari de Consequentibus Augustanae Confessionis insignioribus, quippe has inter alias, Conclusiones formans: Interpretatio Augustanae Confessionis admittit, quicquid ex ea per legitimam Consequentiam deductum est. Item: Religio August. Confess. non ita interpretando coangustanda est, ut totaliter & secundum omnes suos Articulos, in August. Confess. expressa esse dicenda sit, Cap. 2. pag. m. 182. & 200. Scilicet: Quicquid Formulistae vel jam commenti sunt, vel in posterum comminiscentur, istud August. Confess. invariatae Doctrina fuerit, quippe per legitimam consequentiam, (uti ipsis videtur,) ex ea deductum; Quicquid ex adverso, vel Philippus, declarandae ergo Augustanae Confess. à se ipso olim confectae (cujusque proinde interpres, ceu verborum suorum, optimus, videri potest) vel addidit, vel immutavit, Philipistae quoque Pezelius, Sohnius, Crocius, Georgius Pauli, Hoffmannus, Helmstadienses aliique commentantur in Augustanam Confessionem, perque legitimas sibi visas Consequentias inde deducunt, illud ab Augustana Conf. invariata quàm alienissimum habendum. Vel (2.) cum eodem Dorscheo, capite sequenti tertiô, Canones ejusmodi cudunt, qui, ceu à vero haud abludentes, indeque admissi, Variatam Confessionem Philippicam, omnibus aequâ istam lance expendentibus, omnino genuinam ostendunt, & nonnisi odiose, etiam à Dorscheo exagitatam. Variatio, inquit Dorscheus, Augustanae Confessionis quacunque, etiam Substantialis, non debuit alicui transitum ad aliam religionem suadere. Canon. 2. Ergò qui Philippicae adhaeret Confessioni, licèt substantialiter, juxta Dorscheum, variatae, adhuc dum Religioni illi adhaeret, quam Augustana Confessio invariata profitetur, nec Confessio Philippica ad aliam huic Religionem transitum suadet, nedum eundem alteri Religioni addicit. Iterum: Variatio, ait Dorscheus, in Substantiam Veritatis, Articulis Augustanae Confessionis expositae mutationem nullam inferens, non debet odiose exagitari aut causa esse aliquem extra pacem Religionis constituendi. Canon. 3. Item: Variatio, quae suum locum Originalibus exemplaribus relinquit, sinceritati Augustanae Confessionis, non obstat, p. m. 216. 217. 218. Subsumo ego: de Variata Philippica: Non infert haec mutationem in Substantiam Veritatis, [testante Mentzero] relinquit verò locum suum Originalibus Exemplaribus, si quae alicubi supersunt. Ergò.

pass_a.111: §. V. What the Augsburg Confession is, we have clarified by a certain undoubted Description; but of what kind it is, so that we may inquire, its various and varied Editions, and the huge altercations and fights that have arisen about these very things, demand. For either it is an Αὐτόγραφον, or Ἀρχέτυπον, that is, that very Exemplar which was exhibited to the Emperor; and that either Latin only, and therefore unique, mentioned by Chytraeus (History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 81), or rather Latin and German together, and therefore twofold, both described by Celestine (Tom. II pp. 151 and 169). Both Exemplars, after the German Exemplar was read aloud by the Saxon Chancellor Christian Pontanus, were seized by the Emperor hand; the German was given by the Emperor to the Imperial Secretary Alexander Schweiß to be offered to the Elector of Mainz (Celestine Tom. I p. 141 and Tom. III p. 190) and was afterward lodged in the Mainz Archive; the Latin was retained by the Emperor and at last deposited in the Brussels archive. Both lay hidden for many years in the said archives, as Bellarmine witnesses (Judgment on the Book of Concord, Tom. II Controversies p. 485); and that a little later the other [I guess the German] was cut out of the Volume of public Acts then collected at the Augsburg Diet, Dorsche asserts (Dissertation on Divine Providence concerning the Augsburg Confession, held at Rostock in 1555); so that a Genuine Exemplar of the unvaried Augsburg Confession no longer exists today, Bacler rightly inferring so (Memorial cited above, p. 406 at the end). [Note: Justus Jonas writes to Luther, in Chytraeus p. 74 mid-page, that the Emperor had the Augsburg Confession rendered for himself in the Italian and French tongue — which I take to mean transferred into these languages.]
pass_a.112: OR it is an Ἀπόγραφον or ἔκτυπον, that is, a just Exemplar conceived by the pen, understand word for word according to the Original, such as I would not easily deny existed at the time of the Augsburg Diet, since it is hardly probable that neither the Theologians — among them Melanchthon, the chief framer of the Augsburg Confession — nor the Estates of the Empire in whose name the Confession was adorned, had an altogether exact Copy of the Exemplar to be exhibited and exhibited to the Emperor, indeed several procured by the several Estates, and retained and kept for themselves against very various cases; otherwise, if they had done otherwise, they would all to a man be convicted, if not of supine negligence, certainly of a certain stupid lack of foresight; OR finally, a τυπόγραφον or Ἔκτυπον, by the press, that is, copies transcribed in type according to an apograph Exemplar made by the pen — and that either by private venture, such as came out the same year at Breslau in the vernacular in quarto from the types of Adam Dyon, of which Chytraeus (History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 47) pronounces that it was formed after the Original Confession kept in the Mainz Archive, and which the same Chytraeus himself not rarely follows (see the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, p. 6 at the end); or by public authority, such as the next year at Wittenberg several were printed, both German and Latin, both in quarto and in octavo, yet the Latin in quarto obtaining first place among all, even arguing the Breslau one spurious in its preface, as Calov observes (Critica Sacra, p. 82).
pass_a.113: Concerning all these, namely those committed to the press in the first two years, it is certain that they differ in words not rarely both among themselves and from the Autograph: for the earlier verbal difference is proved not only by the Wittenberg Exemplars compared with the Breslau one, but also by the Wittenberg ones among themselves — the Latin in quarto compared with the German of the same format — especially as to Article X, even though both Wittenberg Exemplars used the same Printer Georg Rhau (see Calov Critica pp. 86 to 98). The same is proved by the Exemplars of the Augsburg Confession, both Latin and German, inserted by Chytraeus and Celestine into their Histories; and even by comparing either Author's Latin with his German. E.g. both Celestine's and Chytraeus's German put Article X in these words: [German quote on the Supper under the form of bread and wine]. Tom. II p. 53 b. But the Latin of the same Authors has Article X so formed that no mention at all of the Species of Bread and Wine is injected: They teach concerning the Lord's Supper that the Body and Blood of the Lord are truly present and are distributed to those who eat in the Lord's Supper, and they reject those who teach otherwise. Same Tom. p. 172 b. You may find like discrepancies around Articles XIII and XVIII in the Latin Exemplars of Chytraeus and Celestine compared with each other, inasmuch as the former, the Chytraean, has many additions not found in the Celestinian. So it is no wonder that both Papists and some of the Protestants have from time to time complained of the discrepancy of Exemplars, and Bellarmine does not stray from the truth when in the place cited above he writes that almost every year other and other Exemplars have come out which, though all bore the title of the Augsburg Confession, yet in words and sentences differed much both among themselves and from that first Confession exhibited to the Emperor; or rather Joh. Schmid, convicted by whatever truth there is in Bellarmine's words, charges Bellarmine's diction with hyperbole alone, answering thus: What Bellarmine writes about a change made almost every year is hyperbolic; we do not deny that the Augsburg Confession was changed, but as to words only, not as to the things themselves and the Sentences; we concede that a change was made at the start, by which pact nothing was added to or taken from the essence of the Confession itself: for it is certain that the Augsburg Confession edited at Wittenberg in the year 31, as to Substantial and Doctrinal matters, in no way dissented from the Exemplar exhibited at Augsburg, though as to additions of Phrases and Diction it did not wholly agree with the prototype. Seek the causes of the various changes in Calov Critica and p. 85. The later manifold verbal Difference of printed exemplars — especially of that inserted in the Formula of Concord from the Autograph — the most Illustrious Prince Ernest Frederick, Margrave of Baden, drew out by careful collation in his Christian Reflections and Motives that kept His Princely Grace from subscribing the Formula of Concord (pp. 1 to 98, printed at Castle Staffort in the year 1599).
pass_a.114: §. VI. Printed Exemplars of the Augsburg Confession were followed in succeeding years by many others, until Melanchthon in the years 37 and 38, Luther and the other exhibitors of the Augsburg Confession still living, when he had observed the variety of many copies, both took counsel about publishing a more polished and corrected one and carried it out with no one contradicting — which from many Theologians in the Altenburg colloquy, p. 404, is to prove by this pact that very thing which Calov writes is established by no document (Critica p. 202). See also the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, p. 27 at the end and p. 28. The same Melanchthon undertook to repeat it in the years 1540 and 1542; and in the year 1551 he finished a repetition a third time, but a little more lengthy, and that by order of many Protestant Estates, to be read in Melanchthon's Body of Doctrine — a writing useful and worth reading, so called by Johannes Museus, in which the Doctrine of the Augsburg Confession is declared clearly and elegantly (Lectures on the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, p. 35). And although the earlier two Melanchthon Editions did not have a public Antecedent Approbation, they nevertheless had a Consequent one, both of other Theologians — Chytraeus, Selneccer, Brenz, the Altenburg theologians, and among them Paul Eber, the Meissen men, the Greifswald men, and of Luther himself (Jena German Tom. 7, fol. 447 compared with fol. 448b) — and of the Estates of the Empire in the Conventions at Worms, Regensburg, Frankfurt, and Naumburg, declaring their approbation in the following words: Nor is it our mind, by this repetition and renewed Subscription of the Confession first printed, to depart even in the least from that which was exhibited in the year 40. For since that one, in some Colloquies and Disputations instituted with Adversaries, has been more copiously explained in some Articles precisely so that Heavenly Truth might shine more, and trust in the merit of our Redeemer Jesus Christ might be kept pure and uncorrupted without human traditions and transmitted to posterity, we cannot desert that one any more than the other, especially since that enriched Confession published in type in the years 40 and 42 is now in many hands and is in great part in use in our Churches and Schools.
pass_a.115: All these things our men have pursued at more length — Hospinian, Georg Pauli, Sohn, Ursinus, and others — and in this place especially to be remembered are both the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung from pp. 27 and 57, and also in the appendix or Anhang of the Ausführliche Behauptung from pp. 25 to 36, and our venerable Becmann under the name Orthuinus Gratius against Liebhard, ch. III §2 entire from pp. 73 to 74, who also brings into the open causes of varying the Augsburg Confession that are not to be neglected, from p. 69, and vigorously beats back the exceptions usually leveled at the subsequent Approbation of the varied Confession, in the place cited from pp. 73 to 81, following Crocius, Commentary on Fellowship in the Augsburg Confession, chs. 54–56, with whom he also weakens and eludes both the older or Hutterian cavils in Concordia Concordi pp. 344 and 418 and following, and in Anti-Peucer from p. 7, and the more recent Calovian ones in Critica Sacra from pp. 203 to 228. It will suffice for us here to have noted that even Balthasar Mentzer, a vigorous enough Opponent of the Varied Confession, has candidly acknowledged the subsequent public approbation of it for which we now contend, when in the Prolegomena to the Augsburg Confession, p. 21, he writes thus: Those who admitted the changed Confession have publicly testified that thus far and not otherwise it is received by them, insofar as in the things themselves it plainly agrees with the Prototype, as is clear from the History of the Naumburg Convention, p. 61. Thus far Mentzer; how the Estates of the Empire themselves understood that very point, we saw a little earlier from their Letter written to Ferdinand I. Besides which, even from the words drawn from Mentzer it appears that the Varied Augsburg Confession was held to agree plainly with the Prototype in the things themselves.
pass_a.116: §. VII. So that those men are injurious both to the Augsburg Confession itself and to its nearly chief Author among the Theologians — Melanchthon the best, in his time the Phoenix and easily the Prince of theologians and of all learned Germans alike — who cry that the Varied Edition, as corrupt and depraved, is by no means the same as the original Augsburg Confession but utterly another from it. For that Variation is either Essential, and is said to strike against the Foundation of Faith, and then Philip together with the changed Confession is charged with Heresy; or it is Accidental, and then it plainly agrees with the original in the things themselves, as Mentzer speaks, and is therefore the same with that one. On which account Johann Schmid's answer lodged against Bellarmine, and brought by us in §. V., fits here, to which we add what the same Author subjoins: If, he says, Change and Variation of Words, Diction, and Phrases took away the Confession itself, the case of the Apostles' Creed would long ago have been over, because the monuments testify that it was set forth by other Doctors of the Church in one and another series of words (p. 77 at the end and p. 88). Especially when the Estates of the Empire themselves made no discrimination between the two said Confessions, but reckoned both one and the same (see the Anhang of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 43 to 52). But they are to be held inept who deny that the Variata is Augsburg for this reason, that it was not exhibited at Augsburg — Mentzer drawing the corollary thus: That Confession which was not exhibited at Augsburg ought not to be called Augsburg (Prolegomena n. 9, p. 8), having also gained very many followers here — Schmid in the place cited p. 12, Calov in the same place p. 8, and others. As if truly nothing that was not exhibited at Augsburg could not be called Augustan; or as if the Augsburg Confession denoted or looked to the place and City in which it was made more than the matters and Articles of which it consists (I say the Augsburg Confession does not denote and look to the City in which it was made MORE than the Articles of which it consists, so that I do not deny it could be named from that City and is even to be so named hereafter, though it may chance that [which we most heavily grieve has begun to happen] this Imperial city be reduced to the form of some village); or as if the Confession brought to light at Wittenberg in the year 1531, and not a few other changed ones that by everyone's confession suffered various change, should no longer be Augsburg even for those who scorn and turn from the one varied by Philip, for this reason that they were not exhibited at Augsburg.
pass_a.117: Finally they are found at odds with themselves and all but αὐτοκατάκριτοι, who either (1.) so enlarge the unvaried Augsburg Confession and its Sense that they even say the domestic Doctrines of the Formula of Concord alone — e.g. on the Oral Manducation of the Body of Christ, on the Ubiquity or Omnipresence of the Body of Christ, and the like (of which the Augsburg Confession never even dreamed) — yes, the whole Formula of Concord is comprehended in it, yet with the Philippica Confession, varying in some points, struck out, so as to make room for Brentian interpretations and Consequences, Melanchthonian ones being forbidden and shut out. Where the finger of the otherwise most learned of Lutheran Theologians, and not to be named by me except with veneration, Johann Georg Dorsche, points in his Secular Disputation on the more noted Consequences of the Augsburg Confession, forming among others these Conclusions: The Interpretation of the Augsburg Confession admits whatever has been deduced from it by legitimate Consequence. Also: The Religion of the Augsburg Confession is not to be so narrowed by interpreting that it must be said to be expressed totally and according to all its Articles in the Augsburg Confession (ch. 2, pp. 182 and 200). To wit: Whatever the Formulists have already invented or will invent hereafter will have been the Doctrine of the unvaried Augsburg Confession, inasmuch as deduced from it by legitimate consequence (as it seems to them); whatever on the contrary Philip — for declaring the Augsburg Confession once framed by himself (whose best interpreter, as of his own words, he can therefore seem) — either added or changed, and what the Philippists Pezel, Sohn, Crocius, Georg Pauli, Hoffmann, the Helmstedt men, and others also comment on the Augsburg Confession and deduce thence by consequences that seem legitimate to them, that is to be held most alien from the unvaried Augsburg Confession. Or (2.) with the same Dorsche in the following third chapter they forge Canons of that sort which, as not straying from the truth and therefore admitted, show the Varied Philippica Confession altogether genuine to all who weigh it with an equal balance, and only odiously harassed even by Dorsche. Variation of the Augsburg Confession of whatever kind, says Dorsche, even Substantial, ought not to have persuaded anyone to a passage to another religion (Canon 2). Therefore he who adheres to the Philippica Confession, though substantially varied according to Dorsche, still adheres to that Religion which the unvaried Augsburg Confession professes, and the Philippica Confession does not persuade a passage to another Religion than this, still less binds the same man to another Religion. Again: Variation, says Dorsche, that brings no change into the Substance of Truth set out in the Articles of the Augsburg Confession ought not to be odiously harassed or to be a cause of setting anyone outside the peace of Religion (Canon 3). Also: Variation that leaves their place to the Original exemplars does not stand in the way of the sincerity of the Augsburg Confession (pp. 216, 217, 218). I subsume concerning the Variata Philippica: this does not bring a change into the Substance of Truth [Mentzer bearing witness], but leaves their place to the Original Exemplars, if any still survive anywhere. Therefore.

111: §. V. What the Augsburg Confession is, we have already set out in a clear description.
Of what kind it is — that inquiry is forced on us by its many and altered editions, and by the huge quarrels and pitched fights that have grown up around them.
Either it is an αὐτόγραφον, or ἀρχέτυπον: the very copy shown to the Emperor.
Chytraeus remembers that copy as Latin only, and therefore unique (History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 81).
Celestine rather describes both a Latin and a German together — a pair (Tom. II, pp. 151 and 169).
After the Saxon chancellor Christian Pontanus had read the German aloud, Charles took both copies into his own hand.
He gave the German to his secretary Alexander Schweiß to offer to the Elector of Mainz; it later went into the Mainz archive (Celestine, Tom. I p. 141 and Tom. III p. 190).
He kept the Latin himself and at last lodged it in the Brussels archive.
Both lay hidden for many years in those archives, as Bellarmine notes (Judgment on the Book of Concord, Tom. II, Controversies, p. 485).

Dorsche adds that soon afterward one of them — I guess the German — was cut out of the volume of public acts gathered at the Augsburg Diet (Dissertation on Divine Providence concerning the Augsburg Confession, Rostock 1555).
So a genuine exemplar of the unvaried Confession no longer survives — Bacler rightly draws that conclusion (Memorial cited above, p. 406 at the end).
[Note: Justus Jonas writes Luther, in Chytraeus p. 74 mid-page, that the Emperor had the Confession put into Italian and French for himself; I take that to mean translated into those tongues.]
112: Or it is an ἀπόγραφον — an ἔκτυπον: a fair pen copy, word for word from the original.
I would not easily deny that such copies stood ready at the Augsburg Diet.

It is hardly likely that neither the theologians — Melanchthon chief among the framers — nor the imperial Estates in whose name the Confession was dressed, kept an exact copy of what was shown to Charles, and even several copies procured estate by estate, held back against every sort of chance.
Had they done otherwise, they would one and all stand convicted — if not of lazy neglect, then of a stupid want of foresight.
Or last, a τυπόγραφον — an ἔκτυπον from the press: type set from a pen apograph.

That could be by private venture: the same year a vernacular quarto came out at Breslau from Adam Dyon types. Chytraeus says it was shaped to the original Confession kept in the Mainz archive (History, p. 47), and he himself often follows it (see the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, p. 6 at the end).
Or it could be by public authority: the next year Wittenberg printed several, German and Latin, quarto and octavo.
Among them the Latin quarto took first place, and in its preface even branded the Breslau print a spurious one — as Calov notes (Critica Sacra, p. 82).
113: Of all these first-two-years press copies it is certain: they often differ in wording both from one another and from the autograph.

The earlier verbal split shows not only when Wittenberg copies are set beside the Breslau one, but when Wittenberg copies are set beside each other — the Latin quarto against the German of the same size — above all on Article X, though both Wittenberg runs used the same printer, Georg Rhau (Calov, Critica, pp. 86–98).
The same is proved by the Latin and German exemplars Chytraeus and Celestine put into their histories, and by matching either author's Latin with his German.

Celestine's and Chytraeus's German both cast Article X thus: they teach of the Supper that Christ's true body and blood are truly present under the form of bread and wine, are distributed and received there, and that the contrary teaching is rejected (Tom. II, p. 53b).

But their Latin forms Article X so that the species of bread and wine are never named: they teach concerning the Lord's Supper that the body and blood of the Lord are truly present and are distributed to those who eat, and they reject those who teach otherwise (same Tom., p. 172b).
Like gaps turn up around Articles XIII and XVIII when Chytraeus's and Celestine's Latin copies are compared: Chytraeus has many additions Celestine lacks.
No wonder, then, that Papists and some Protestants have complained of discrepant copies.

Bellarmine is not far from the truth when he writes (in the place already cited) that almost every year new exemplars appeared which, though all wore the Augsburg title, differed much in words and sentences both among themselves and from the first Confession shown to Charles.

Johann Schmid, pressed by whatever truth sits in those words, answers that Bellarmine's yearly-change talk is hyperbole alone: we do not deny verbal change, but we deny change of the things and sentences; an early change we grant, yet by that pact nothing was added to or taken from the Confession's essence.

The Wittenberg edition of 1531, he says, did not dissent from the Augsburg-exhibited exemplar in substance or doctrine, though its added phrases and diction did not wholly match the prototype. For the causes of the various changes, see Calov, Critica, and p. 85.

Later, the many verbal differences among printed copies — above all the Formula of Concord insert set against the autograph — were carefully collated by the most illustrious prince Ernest Frederick, Margrave of Baden, in the Christian Reflections and Motives that kept His Princely Grace from subscribing the Formula (pp. 1–98, printed at Castle Staffort, 1599).
114: §. VI. In the years that followed, many other printed copies of the Augsburg Confession came after the first.

Then in 1537 and 1538 — Luther and the other original exhibitors still alive — Melanchthon, seeing how the many copies varied, took counsel to issue a more polished and corrected edition, and carried it out with no one contradicting.
Many theologians at the Altenburg colloquy (p. 404) thus prove the very point Calov says no document establishes (Critica, p. 202). See also the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 27–28.
Melanchthon undertook the same again in 1540 and 1542.

In 1551, by order of many Protestant Estates, he finished a third and somewhat longer repeat, to be read in his Body of Doctrine — a useful writing worth reading, says Johannes Museus, in which Augsburg doctrine is set out clearly and with elegance (Lectures on the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, p. 35).
The earlier two Melanchthon editions lacked a public approval beforehand; they still won approval afterward.

Other theologians owned them — Chytraeus, Selneccer, Brenz, the Altenburg men, among them Paul Eber, the Meissen and Greifswald faculties — and Luther himself (Jena German Tom. 7, fol. 447 with 448b).
So did the imperial Estates in the diets at Worms, Regensburg, Frankfurt, and Naumburg, declaring in these words:
Nor is it our mind, by this repetition and renewed subscription of the Confession first printed, to depart even in the least from that shown in the year 40.

For in some colloquies and disputations with adversaries that later text was explained more fully in certain articles, so that heavenly truth might shine the more, and trust in the merit of our Redeemer Jesus Christ might be kept pure and uncorrupted without human traditions and handed on to posterity.
We cannot desert that enriched Confession any more than the other — especially since the 1540 and 1542 print now sits in many hands and is largely in use in our churches and schools.
115: Our own writers have chased all this out at more length — Hospinian, Georg Pauli, Sohn, Ursinus, and the rest.

Here I mark especially the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung (pp. 27 and 57; and the Anhang, pp. 25–36), and our own venerable Becmann under the name Orthuinus Gratius against Liebhard (ch. III §2, pp. 73–74 entire).

Becmann also brings forward causes for varying the Augsburg Confession that deserve a hearing (from p. 69), and he beats back hard the stock objections aimed at the Variata's later approval (pp. 73–81), following Crocius on Augsburg fellowship (chs. 54–56).
With Crocius he also drains and turns aside both the older Hutterian cavils (Concordia Concordi, pp. 344 and 418ff.; Anti-Peucer from p. 7) and the newer Calovian ones (Critica Sacra, pp. 203–228).
For us it is enough to note this: even Balthasar Mentzer, a sturdy enough foe of the Variata, candidly owns the later public approval for which we now argue.

In his Prolegomena to the Augsburg Confession (p. 21) he writes: those who admitted the changed Confession have publicly testified that they receive it thus far and no otherwise — insofar as in the things themselves it plainly agrees with the prototype, as the History of the Naumburg Convention shows (p. 61).
So Mentzer. How the imperial Estates themselves took that point, we saw a little earlier in their letter to Ferdinand I.
And even Mentzer's own words make plain that the Varied Augsburg Confession was held to agree with the prototype in the things themselves.
116: §. VII. Those who cry that the Variata is corrupt and depraved — not the same as the original Augsburg Confession, but utterly another — do injury both to the Confession itself and to Melanchthon, its near-chief theological author, in his day the phoenix and easy prince of Germany's theologians and learned men.

For that variation is either essential, and is said to strike the foundation of faith — and then Philip, together with the changed Confession, is charged with heresy — or it is only accidental, and then it plainly agrees with the original in the things themselves, as Mentzer puts it, and is therefore the same confession.
Johann Schmid's answer to Bellarmine, which we already cited in §. V., fits here; and we add what he subjoins:

If change of words, diction, and phrases took away the Confession itself, the Apostles' Creed would long ago have been done for — the monuments show church doctors set it out in one wording and another (pp. 77 end and 88).
Above all, the imperial Estates themselves drew no line between the two Confessions, but counted both one and the same (Anhang of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 43–52).

Inept, too, are those who deny the Variata the name Augsburg because it was not shown at Augsburg — Mentzer's corollary (Prolegomena n. 9, p. 8), with a crowd of followers: Schmid (p. 12), Calov (p. 8), and others.
As if nothing not exhibited at Augsburg could bear an Augustan name; or as if the Augsburg Confession pointed more to the city where it was made than to the matters and articles of which it consists.

(I say it does not mark the city MORE than the articles — without denying it could take its name from that city and should still do so hereafter, even if, as we most heavily grieve has begun, that imperial city should shrink toward the shape of a village.)

Or as if the Confession published at Wittenberg in 1531, and not a few other altered prints that everyone owns suffered various change, ceased to be Augsburg even for those who scorn Philip's Variata — merely because they were not shown at Augsburg.
117: Finally these opponents are caught at odds with themselves — all but αὐτοκατάκριτοι.

(1.) They stretch the unvaried Augsburg Confession and its sense so wide that they even fold into it the Formula of Concord's household doctrines — oral manducation of Christ's body, ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ's body, and the like — of which the Augsburg Confession never so much as dreamed — yes, the whole Formula, they say, is packed inside it.
Yet they strike out the Philippica Confession where it varies in some points, so as to make room for Brentian readings and consequences while Melanchthon's are barred and shut out.

Where the finger of Johann Georg Dorsche points — otherwise among the most learned Lutheran divines, and a name I speak only with reverence — in his Secular Disputation on the more noted consequences of the Augsburg Confession, forming among others these conclusions:
Interpretation of the Augsburg Confession admits whatever is drawn from it by legitimate consequence.
Also: Augsburg religion is not to be so narrowed by interpreting that it must be said to be expressed wholly, and in all its articles, inside the Augsburg Confession itself (ch. 2, pp. 182 and 200).
In plain: whatever the Formulists have already spun, or will invent later, is to count as unvaried Augsburg doctrine — because deduced, as they see it, by legitimate consequence.

But whatever Philip added or changed in declaring the Confession he himself once framed — and he may well seem its best interpreter, as of his own words — and whatever Philippists (Pezel, Sohn, Crocius, Georg Pauli, Hoffmann, the Helmstedt men, and others) comment and draw by consequences that seem legitimate to them, that is to be held most alien from the unvaried Confession.

(2.) Or with the same Dorsche in the next, third chapter they mint canons which, if admitted as not far from the truth, show the Variata Philippica altogether genuine to anyone who weighs it with an even hand — and only odiously harassed, even by Dorsche.
Variation of the Augsburg Confession of whatever kind, says Dorsche, even substantial, ought not to have talked anyone into crossing to another religion (Canon 2).

Therefore he who holds to the Philippica, though Dorsche calls it substantially varied, still holds to the religion the unvaried Augsburg Confession professes; the Philippica does not urge a crossing to another religion, still less binds a man to one.
Again: variation that brings no change into the substance of truth set out in the Augsburg articles ought not to be odiously harassed or used to push anyone outside the peace of religion (Canon 3).
Also: variation that leaves the original exemplars their place does not block the sincerity of the Augsburg Confession (pp. 216–218).
I subsume for the Variata Philippica: it brings no change into the substance of truth — Mentzer is witness — and it leaves the original exemplars their place, if any still survive. Therefore.
